sources.fullCitation: [Photograph of Robert Katscher, Armin Robinson, Paul Whiteman, Erwin Hein, Fritz Wreede and Otto Hein]. Photos Willinger. Die Bühne (Vienna), no. 85 (1926): 12, with the article “Jazz und die Wiener Komponisten”. Österreichische Nationalbibliothek / ANNO.
sources.title: Armin Robinson with Paul Whiteman and Robert Katscher — Die Bühne, 1926
sources.researchNote: The photograph belongs to “Jazz und die Wiener Komponisten”, a page of statements by Viennese authors published for Paul Whiteman’s visit to the city, and is credited with the page’s other picture to the Willinger studio. The printed caption reads “Von links nach rechts: Dr. Robert Katscher, Armin Robinson, Paul Whiteman, Direktor Erwin Hein, Fritz Wreede, Direktor Otto Hein”, and six men are visible. Whiteman is certain: the same page prints him again, named, beside Katscher at a piano. Counting from the left he is third, which agrees with the caption and would make the second figure — balding, in round spectacles — Armin Robinson, then twenty-six years old. A portrait published elsewhere as Robinson shows a man with full dark hair and no spectacles, so the archive does not say which face here is his. The page carries the printed number 12; ANNO serves it as page 14, which is the address the link uses.
sources.creator: Willinger

media.title: Armin Robinson with Paul Whiteman and Robert Katscher, Vienna, 1926
media.description: Photograph printed in the Viennese weekly Die Bühne in 1926, on a page of statements by Viennese authors published for Paul Whiteman’s visit to the city. It shows the American bandleader among Viennese musicians and publishers, the lyricist Armin Robinson among them; Robinson wrote the words of three songs Kaper composed in Berlin between 1930 and 1931.
media.altText: Six men crowded together in a bar, one of them stout and smiling with a glass raised, another with his arm around the shoulders of a man in a light suit, with bottles on shelves behind them.
media.rightsNote: Public domain. The photograph appeared in an Austrian magazine in 1926 under the studio credit “Photos Willinger”: the Austrian term for a simple photograph, which a reception snapshot is, runs fifty years from publication and expired in 1976.
